questions.prompt: 28 successes in 30 episodes. Lower bound of the 95 % Wilson interval, 3 decimals.
questions.skillLabel: Judge success rates with the Wilson bound

questions.prompt: 45 successes in 50 episodes. Lower bound of the 95 % Wilson interval, 3 decimals.
questions.skillLabel: Judge success rates with the Wilson bound

questions.prompt: All 30 episodes succeed. Which claim is justified?
options: At least about 88 % (95 % confidence); 100 % is not proven.
The success rate is exactly 100 %, because no episode failed in the sample.
The robot can never fail in simulation, since the sample had no failure.
The benchmark is too easy to tell us anything, so it can be ignored.
questions.explanation: The Wilson lower bound for 30/30 is 0.886. A perfect sample still leaves uncertainty.
questions.skillLabel: Judge success rates with the Wilson bound

questions.prompt: Circumscribed radius 0.18 m, margin 0.04 m, position sigma 0.05 m (use 2 sigma). Inflation radius in 5 cm cells, rounded up.
The goal lies inside a lethal (inflated) cell. What should the navigator do?
options: Plan to it anyway and let the tracker stop at the inflation boundary.
Delete the obstacle from the map so that the goal becomes a free cell.
Snap to the nearest free cell, or report no_path and say why.
Lower the inflation radius to zero for this one episode only.
questions.explanation: A goal inside lethal space is unreachable by construction. Snapping with a logged reason or failing explicitly keeps the result interpretable; the other options hide a bug or reduce safety.

questions.prompt: Octile heuristic for dx = 40 and dy = 15 cells (cells, 2 decimals).
Why is Manhattan distance a poor heuristic for A* on an 8-connected grid?
options: It is far too expensive to compute at every single node of the search.
It does not depend on the goal position, so A* degenerates.
It cannot be computed from integer cell indices on a regular grid.
It overestimates diagonal moves, so it is inadmissible: A* may return a longer path.
questions.explanation: For dx = 24, dy = 10 Manhattan gives 34 but the true free-space cost is 28.14.

questions.prompt: A cell is crossed by 4 free beams with p_free = 0.4 (starting at p = 0.5). Occupancy probability, 3 decimals.
Why clamp cell log-odds to a range such as [-4, 4]?
options: So the grid can be stored as 8-bit integers only.
So a cell that was marked wrongly, or a door that opened, can change its mind within a few scans.
So the probabilities always sum to one across the grid.
So the inverse sensor model can be skipped.
questions.explanation: Unbounded evidence makes a cell stubborn: after hundreds of hits it would need hundreds of free readings to flip.

questions.prompt: Lookahead point at (0.6, 0.2) m in the robot frame. Curvature kappa = 2 y / L^2 in 1/m.
v = 0.4 m/s, deceleration 0.8 m/s^2, total latency 200 ms. Stopping distance in metres.
A heading error of 1.5 degrees while mapping a wall 4 m away. Sideways error of the wall cells in metres, 3 decimals.
questions.explanation: 4 * tan(1.5 deg) = 0.105 m, about two 5 cm cells.
questions.skillLabel: Pose error spreads into the map

questions.prompt: Design the checks that prove the navigation code never uses simulator ground truth.

Dynamic check: give the navigator an env wrapper that exposes only observe(), or perturb the truth and confirm the result does not change.
Names a failure case the checks would catch (for example reading the world occupancy grid instead of lidar) and what test fails.

Includes edge cases (start equals goal, goal blocked) and records expansions to see the heuristic's benefit.

questions.prompt: An obstacle appears 1.5 m ahead while the robot follows a path. Describe the behaviour your navigator should show and what it logs.
rubric: Detects the obstacle in the next scan, marks it in the costmap and stops or slows when the inflated cost ahead becomes lethal.
Replans a bounded number of times and returns blocked with a reason when no path exists; no endless oscillation.
Logs the minimum clearance and the outcome so the acceptance test can check them.

questions.prompt: The robot must pass a 0.9 m wide door. Explain how growing pose covariance should change your planner's behaviour.
rubric: Computes the inflated free width from the footprint, margin and 2 sigma and shows when the door becomes impassable.
Prefers relocalising (landmarks) or slowing before the door to shrinking sigma, rather than silently blocking.
Reports a distinct failure reason such as localisation uncertain, not a generic timeout.
